source.title: Nested Sparsity for Scalable Pretraining and Continual Learning
source.authors: Tian-Zhe Chu; Druv Pai; Y. Ma

record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out language-model cross-entropy across model scales and fits loss-versus-compute power laws, using a related scaling-law method on new architectures.
record.gate_note: The pretraining scale sweep and the architecture-schedule ablation report the study's own held-out-loss results. Continued-pretraining and domain-adaptation losses are not rows because the study does not test power-law behavior in those regimes. Cited scaling-law results from other work are not rows.
record.test_reason: An architecture paper that uses L(F)=A·F^-α+L∞ fits mainly as a tool to estimate compute multipliers. It still reports its own held-out pretraining losses for dense, MoE, NESTOR and sliding-window models across four scales (0.02–3.49 PFLOP/s-days, about 2.2 orders of compute), and each curve is fitted by a power law plus offset. That bears weakly on V1 in new architectures. It is not T1: compute follows a fixed 50 tokens/active-parameter path, there are only four points per three-parameter fit, and no goodness-of-fit is reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, but incomplete. The authors conclude that NESTOR reaches lower held-out loss than MoE and dense baselines at every scale from 100M to 1B active parameters. The MoE needs 1.13–1.29× and the dense model 3.1–4.1× the compute to match it, with no downward trend across the four scales. They also report better domain adaptation with less forgetting and a growing long-context advantage at equal FLOPs. The schedule/layer-order effects are an appendix ablation used to choose the design, not a headline conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: The study fits held-out loss against training compute using L(F) = A F^-α + L∞ and compares several architectures, but does not independently sweep parameter count, tokens, or compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Held-out loss changes with the active-column schedule and the order of layers. Primary scaling comparisons use 50 tokens per active parameter.

fits_no_version.finding: The column-sparsity schedule and its layer order change held-out loss at fixed active compute: from 3.088 up to 3.582 nats (Kc=2), and by about 0.03 nats from order alone with matched layers and storage.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In routed-attention architectures, loss depends on how attention sparsity is distributed over depth at fixed compute.

fits_no_version.finding: Fitted compute exponents differ by architecture variant: 0.092 for dense, 0.101 for MoE and NESTOR, 0.099–0.125 for sliding-window MoE, and 0.114/0.164 for attention-residual ablations. Offsets trade off against exponents.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fitted loss-compute exponents and offsets depend on architecture and are poorly constrained by few-point fits.

record.code_released: GitHub availability is stated, but no URL is given in the text.
record.problems: The primary scale comparisons report no uncertainty estimates and use one seed per model/scale. The fitted curves cover four model scales, and the study does not validate predictions from small runs against much larger runs. Schedule comparisons vary stored parameter counts in several conditions.

untested.parts: Separate scaling in parameters and in tokens. Ranges beyond about 2.2 orders of compute. Goodness-of-fit or residuals of the power-law form, given only four points per three-parameter fit.
No fit on small runs validated against much larger runs.
No search for the compute-optimal N/D split; a fixed 50 tokens/parameter is used.
Systematic depth/width variation over a wide range at fixed parameter count in standard transformers.
Continual pretraining, repeated data and domain adaptation are run, but no power-law fits are made in those regimes.
No variation of fitting method, parameter counting or schedule; curve bending is not examined.

missing.what: Configuration-search losses at the 200M scale: alternative layer splits and wider attention or wider experts instead of more layers, 0.004–0.033 nats higher.
MoE with twice the experts at half width, same loss as the baseline (3.107 vs 3.108/3.113).
Attention-residual ablation fits across four scales: L=1.20F^-0.114+1.61 and L=0.73F^-0.164+2.01.
Capacity law in stored parameters at fixed active compute: L=2.970+0.118N^-0.698 for MoE expert-count runs.

record.verdict_notes: The power-law fits are a measurement tool for compute multipliers, not a test of the law. There are four points per three-parameter fit, one seed per scale (two at 200M), and no residuals. The authors' Appendix E assumes a Hoffmann-style law as a hypothesis. They say separate offsets are not allowed by their proposition, and that a lower L∞ makes the multiplier grow. Rows r1–r12 are single points and only jointly bear on V1. The V4 rows were relinked to none because sparsity schedule is not the depth/width shape that V4 names.

versions.untested_parts: Parameters and tokens are not varied independently of compute; models follow a fixed 50 tokens per active parameter training path. The primary sweep covers four scales, from 100M to 1B active parameters.
The study does not fit laws only on small runs and then validate predictions against much larger runs.
No sweep searches for the loss-minimising parameter/token allocation at fixed compute.

The study varies column sparsity schedules and layer order, not depth and width independently across a broad range. Schedule comparisons hold active scale and compute approximately fixed, but stored parameter counts can differ.
Continual pretraining, repeated data, and domain adaptation are evaluated, but the study does not test whether their loss curves follow the same power-law form.
No downstream task performance is evaluated.
The study does not vary fitting choices or test whether exponents or compute-optimal allocations depend on those choices, nor does it test curves bending away from a single law.
